h1:
Khao Phra Wihan National Park
Pha Mo E Daeng, the Twin Stupa, and a Border Nature Trail
intro: Khao Phra Wihan National Park sits on the highest cliff edge of southern Isan, looking out over the Cambodian plains as far as the eye can see. The headliners are Pha Mo E Daeng, a thousand-year-old sandstone Twin Stupa, the relief carvings tucked under the cliff face, and a short nature trail through wild orchids. But because it lies right on the Thailand–Cambodia border, you have to check the situation every single time before you go — the area sometimes closes for safety. So we've pulled together both what's worth seeing and what you need to know before setting off, all in one place.

⚠️ Check the border before you go

blocks.title: Read this before you plan — the border situation
blocks.html: Khao Phra Wihan National Park and the Pha Mo E Daeng viewpoint sit right on the Thailand–Cambodia border. In the past there have been notices to temporarily close Pha Mo E Daeng after tensions flared along the frontier, for visitors' safety. Before every trip, call the park headquarters (tel. 0 4582 6045) or check the Khao Phra Wihan National Park Facebook page and the latest border news. Don't rely on old photos in reviews — the open/closed status can change fast. Always have a backup plan.

Khao Phra Wihan National Park straddles Kantharalak District in Sisaket and Nam Yuen District in Ubon Ratchathani, covering roughly 130 square kilometres. Its southern edge follows the Phanom Dong Rak mountain range, which marks the border with Cambodia. The first thing most people picture is Pha Mo E Daeng, a sandstone cliff about 300 metres long where you can stand and look out across the Cambodian plains. Nearby there are also small ancient ruins that are older than the Preah Vihear temple itself, which makes this both a viewpoint, a historical site, and a patch of wild nature all at once.

blocks.text: Pha Mo E Daeng, the clifftop viewpoint

blocks.html: Pha Mo E Daeng is the steep cliff that anchors the whole park. A wide rock terrace lets you walk along the edge for about 300 metres, looking down over the forest and the Cambodian plains in a long panorama. On some evenings you'll see a stream of bats pouring out of a cave below the cliff — people who come late in the day like to wait around for it. The wind up on the cliff is strong and the sun is fully exposed, so bring a hat and water, and stay on the marked path the rangers set out, because some spots are close to the border line and areas that still need caution.

items: Border view — a wide look down over the Cambodian plains and the Phanom Dong Rak range
Evening bats — on some days a stream of bats flies out of the cave below the cliff around sunset
Strong wind, harsh sun — it's an open rock terrace, so bring a hat, sunglasses, and drinking water
Stay on the marked path — some spots are near the border, so keep to the trail and follow ranger advice

blocks.text: The relief carvings below Pha Mo E Daeng

blocks.html: Below the Pha Mo E Daeng cliff there's a relief carving on the sandstone wall — three life-sized deities, thought to be around 1,000–1,500 years old, older than the Preah Vihear temple up on the summit. It's evidence that people used this area long before the temple was built. To go down and see it you have to take a stairway down along the cliff, and some sections may be closed depending on the situation, so ask the rangers at the service point first whether it's open to go down that day.

blocks.text: The Twin Stupa, a sandstone ruin

blocks.html: West of Pha Mo E Daeng stands the Twin Stupa, a pair of cube-shaped ruins built from sandstone, sitting side by side, about 1.9 metres wide and roughly 4 metres tall. They're in the Khmer style and symbolise fertility, with a yoni base and a lingam as part of the structure. Set in the middle of an open rock terrace, they're an easy walk to reach and a spot people like to stop and photograph against the wide sky.

items: Built from sandstone — two square stupas side by side, ancient Khmer style
Size — about 1.9 metres wide, roughly 4 metres tall, with a yoni base and lingam
Easy to reach — not far from the Pha Mo E Daeng terrace, a popular photo spot

blocks.text: Waterfalls and nature in the park

blocks.html: Beyond the cliff and the ruins, the park also has small waterfalls and streams running through deciduous dipterocarp and dry evergreen forest. The waterfalls inside the park run highest late in the rainy season, around August to October, while in the dry season the water drops off a lot. If you're set on seeing the waterfalls, pick the period after the rains and check with the rangers first that the trail is open and safe to walk, because some routes run deep into the forest near the border and may close when the situation isn't normal.

The park has a short nature trail of about 1.5 kilometres, focused on wild orchids and the many medicinal plants that grow on the rock terraces and in the shade. It's an easy walk, not too steep, and works for all ages who just want a gentle stroll through nature. The orchids bloom prettiest from late rainy season into early winter. Wear shoes with good grip, since some stretches of rock get slippery after rain, and carry your own water because refill points are limited.

items: Distance — about 1.5 kilometres, not steep, suits all ages
Highlight — wild orchids and medicinal plants on the rock terraces, prettiest late rainy season to early winter
Come prepared — shoes with good grip, bring your own water, the rock gets slippery after rain

blocks.text: Entry fees, hours, and getting there

blocks.html: The park charges entry at the standard Department of National Parks rate — Thai adults around 40 THB, children around 20 THB, foreign adults around 400 THB, children around 200 THB, plus a vehicle fee depending on the type. Opening hours are generally around 08:00–16:30, but if you want to stay into the evening to wait for the bats, you'll need to ask the rangers how late visitors are allowed that day. The easiest way to get here is to drive yourself: it's about 100 kilometres from Sisaket town heading toward Kantharalak District, with the final stretch climbing up the mountain, so check your vehicle and fill up the tank before you start the climb.

items: Entry fee — Thai adults around ฿40, children around ฿20 · foreign adults around ฿400, children around ฿200 (rates may change, check on site)
Hours — around 08:00–16:30 · to stay into the evening for the bats, ask the rangers
Getting there — driving yourself is easiest, about 100 km from Sisaket town to Kantharalak, with a mountain climb at the end
Contact — park headquarters tel. 0 4582 6045 (check the open/closed status before you go)

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: This isn't a place you can just show up at without planning — between the distance, the mountain climb, and most of all the open/closed status that hinges on the border situation. Sometimes Pha Mo E Daeng is closed for long stretches, but other spots in the province like the Khmer temples or the volcanic-soil durian orchards are still open to visit. If you call to check and it's closed, don't feel bad — switch the plan to somewhere else and come back when things are normal. That's the better call.

If the border situation is normal and the park is open, here's a rough plan that pairs Khao Phra Wihan with other things to do around Kantharalak, to make the long drive worth it. Adjust the timing as needed, and always keep a backup ready in case one spot is closed.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Into Sisaket town, then south to Kantharalak

items.activity: Arrive in Sisaket town and have khanom chin or a local breakfast to fuel up before setting off
items.note: Check the border news and call the park to confirm it's open one more time

items.activity: Drive south to Kantharalak District, stopping at a volcanic-soil durian orchard in season (around June–August) or a local Isan restaurant along the way
items.note: It's about 100 km from town, so allow extra time for the mountain climb

items.activity: Head up into Khao Phra Wihan National Park to walk Pha Mo E Daeng, the Twin Stupa, and the relief carvings (if it's open to go down)
items.note: Stay on the marked path and follow ranger advice

items.activity: Wait for the sunset and the bats on the cliff if visitors are allowed to stay late that day, then come down to stay in the Kantharalak area
items.note: If the cliff closes in the evening, come down for dinner in town instead

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Nature trail, Khmer temple, back to town

items.activity: Walk the wild orchid nature trail in the park, about 1.5 km, or stop by a waterfall if it's the post-rain season
items.note: Check with the rangers that the trail is open and safe to walk

items.activity: Drive back north, stopping at a Khmer temple along the way, such as the temples around the Kantharalak–town area
items.note: A good backup plan if the park is closed

items.activity: Head back into Sisaket town and pick up local souvenirs like shallots, garlic, and regional snacks
items.note: Sisaket souvenirs are known for shallots, garlic, and volcanic-soil durian in season

blocks.text: What to bring to Khao Phra Wihan

items: ID card or passport, since it's a border area and there may be checkpoints
Drinking water and a hat — the cliff terrace has harsh sun and strong wind
Walking shoes with good grip — the rock gets slippery after rain
Cash for the entry fee and the shops at the park entrance — phone signal is weak in some spots
The park headquarters' number to call and check the status before and during the trip

faq.q: Are Khao Phra Wihan National Park and Pha Mo E Daeng open to visit right now?
faq.a: The open/closed status depends on the Thailand–Cambodia border situation. In the past there have been notices to temporarily close Pha Mo E Daeng for safety. Before every trip, call the park headquarters at 0 4582 6045 or check the Khao Phra Wihan National Park Facebook page and the latest news. Don't go by old photos in reviews.

faq.q: Are Khao Phra Wihan and Preah Vihear temple the same place?
faq.a: They're not the same place. On the Thai side, Khao Phra Wihan National Park has Pha Mo E Daeng, the Twin Stupa, and the relief carvings, while the Preah Vihear temple itself sits on the summit in Cambodian territory. Visiting the temple depends on agreements and the border situation, and for long stretches it isn't open to access from the Thai side.

faq.q: How much is the entry fee for Khao Phra Wihan National Park?
faq.a: The standard rate is around 40 THB for Thai adults, around 20 THB for children, around 400 THB for foreign adults, and around 200 THB for children, plus a vehicle fee by type. Rates may change, so check again at the service point on site.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Khao Phra Wihan?
faq.a: Late rainy season into early winter, roughly October to February — the weather is cool, the views are clear, and it's when the wild orchids bloom. If you want to see the waterfalls running full, come in the post-rain period around August to October. Avoid midday in the hot season, when the cliff terrace gets very harsh sun.

faq.q: How do you get to Khao Phra Wihan, and is it possible without a private car?
faq.a: The easiest way is to drive yourself or rent a car — it's about 100 kilometres from Sisaket town heading toward Kantharalak District, with a mountain climb at the end. Without a private car you may need to charter a vehicle from town or Kantharalak, since public transport reaching the park is limited.
